Analog Man King of Tone Review Posted by hallamkite February 23, 2016 Home The King Of Tone is among the most desirable pedals on the planet. Its reputation is built upon its open nature, touch-sensitivity and the quality of its organic sounding overdrive. The KOT has two sides that can be used independently and set to ‘clean boost’, ‘mild gain’ or ‘high gain’ via internal dip switches giving it a valuable level of versatility. Used on its own the KOT is clear and precise, it is reminiscent of more common overdrive pedals but it delivers a more even response across the EQ spectrum. This is definitely a low-medium gain pedal, which suits me perfectly, but I wouldn’t suggest it to someone after more modern hi-gain rock tones. Used as a clean boost it doesn’t colour your signal, but it really is at its best when you dial in a touch of that wonderful grit. Being able to stack the two sides is incredibly useful, especially in a live setting. I would be inclined to use the dip switches to set the right-hand side to ‘medium gain’ and the left-hand side to ‘clean boost’, this would give me all the boosting options I need. I wouldn’t employ the KOT as an always-on pedal. The nature of its drive isn’t what I go for as a base level of light break-up. I’d rather use the amp itself or a pedal more like the ZVEX Box of Rock for that. In fact my favourite results were when I ran the KOT as a boost into the Box of Rock, it sounded absolutely awesome, which cements my opinion that the KOT is really best as a lead boost. Overall, the King of Tone’s clarity and responsiveness are really something and I’d happily incorporate into my rig. It certainly hands out the beat-downs to all but the most refined of overdrive pedals. The KoT is designed for the player who wants you to hear as much of his guitar, and even his fingers, as possible. If that sounds like you then you owe it to yourself to hunt one down. Visit the Analog Man website for the full story behind the King Of Tone: www.analogman.com Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Like Loading... Analog Man browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive distortion browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive overdrive browse by enclosure pedal Analog Man King Of Tone Published on February 14, 2006 Analog Man distortion overdrive pedal Only 1 of these was ever made and auctioned to help the victims of the 2011 earthquake and tsunami that hit Japan Gold version Information Analog.Man Analog Man, in collaboration with Jim Weider, have come out with the pedal we have been looking for for many years - the King Of Tone (KoT). There are many overdrive pedals on the market, but none of them have been quite right, preserving the tone of the guitar and adding the right amount of overdrive without compromise. There are some good clean boosts available, but they just don't have enough drive to really give your amp the distortion you often want. There are some newer OD pedals that have a great frequency response, but to me they sound too DRY, sterile, and cardboardy. That is where the King Of Tone pedal comes in - it has enough warm overdrive but still preserves the tones of your quality guitars and amps. Jim had been using an original TS-808 for well over 20 years, it's now housed in a 1980s TS9 case after Rick Danko stepped on it at a concert that THE BAND played. Jim likes the tone of his TS-808, but has always found it loses some low end and is a bit too heavy in the mids. I also love TS808s and have sold thousands of TS9s with our TS808 mods. But sometimes I have wished for a less compressed, more open and natural sound with more of the guitar's actual tone, or as Jim says "you can hear the note better". A Tube Screamer makes it easier to play and sound good due to the compression and vocal midrange boost, but a master player like Jim would often prefer less coloration to allow his techniques and superb tone to get through. The King Of Tone overdrive was designed to take an amp at reasonable settings, and make it sound like it would sound if it were naturally driven to pure, smooth, tube distortion. It was fine tuned with Jim's 1960s Fender Deluxe Reverb amp to duplicate the sound when his amp is singing, but at lower volume settings - to simulate the natural tube amp distortion of preamp and power tubes.
